newsitem.title: USA: No error in U.S. Q4 ECI figure - Labor Dept's Barron.
newsitem.headline: No error in U.S. Q4 ECI figure - Labor Dept's Barron.

text.p: A top official with the U.S. Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics denied speculation that errors were made in the calculation of Tuesday's fourth-quarter Employment Cost Index figure.
"There are no errors in the figure," BLS Deputy Commissioner Bill Barron told Reuters.
The department said earlier Tuesday that the Employment Cost Index rose 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter of last year -- a smaller gain than many economists had been expecting.

The index, a broad measure of employee compensation costs that includes fringe benefits, has been closely watched in financial markets amid belief that it could be an important factor for the Federal Reserve as it considers whether to raise interest rates.

U.S. stock and bond markets initially rallied on the tamer-than-expected fourth-quarter ECI. But the markets pared their gains in part because of rumors that there may have been inaccuracies in the ECI that caused it to understate compensation trends.
One particular point of focus was the finance, insurance and real estate component of the index, which posted a 0.6 percent drop in the fourth quarter.
Some private analysts felt the drop was improbable given the widely reported large bonuses on Wall Street.
Barron said the statistical sample for that component is very small, causing it to be highly erratic from quarter to quarter.
He said that, given the variance, it was worth evaluating whether the finance, insurance and real estate component should even be included in the index.
"The variance of that component is very high and always has been so that maybe we should not even include it. It is maybe something we should look at," he said.

Still, Barron stressed that the component itself is a very small part of the index and that even if it had not shown a decline for the fourth quarter, the difference it would have made for the overall ECI would not have been statistically significant.
